I do not complain for one of the patronage going to the Liberals of this country under our present system, but I do complain of the minister claiming that he is benefiting the workingmen of Canada when he is simply benefiting his own partisans.
On what authority did the Minister of Public Works erect a building costing over $5,000 without letting it out by contract ?
I stated that the building had been erected under the supervision of a man who is a strong political opponent of purs.
By day's labour ?
Yes. It could not be done any other way.
The minister must know that the law of the land prevents him from doing that.
No.
The statutory law makes it incumbent on you to give a contract for any building costing over $5,000.
There is no law of that kind.

There is an Order in Council which in a sense is higher than a statute, because it has been approved by the government itself. I have heard that principle contended for time and time again when the Liberals were in opposition, but perhaps they have disregarded their principles more in this than even in other matters. I always understood that we asked

the minister if the work would be given by contract whenever a vote was taken, but perhaps we did not do so in this case.
SIR CHARLES HIBBERT TUPPER. Here is the Order in Council.
I know the Order in Council very well.

This Order in Council states :
Order in Council, May 23rd, 1880. On a Joint memorandum, dated March 20th, 1880, from the Honourable the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Railways and Canals, recommending that hereafter all public works involving an expenditure of over $5,000 shall be let by public tender and contract, unless owing to urgency or other cause it be deemed advisable to take different action, and that in all such cases authority be obtained by an Order in Council.
Probably the Minister of Public Works did not even get an Order in Council passed. All expenditures such as this are illegal except in the case of a canal breaking or some work of emergency. The Minister of Public Works disregards Acts of parliament, Orders in Council and everything else. I do not know of any possible way of keeping him within the principles which were so earnestly advocated by his friends when in opposition. An Act of parliament won't do it, an Order in Council won't do it, and I don't suppose we can secure a vote of censure from the House on the conduct of the hon. minister.

I do not think that my hon. friend could get the censure of the House, because there is no ground for it. The hon. gentleman is altogether mistaken in his interpretation of the law. I invite him to read it; it is very clear :
The minister shall invite tenders by public advertisement for the execution of all works, except in eases of pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest or in which from the nature of the work it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers in the service of the department.
The minister is perfectly free.
What are you quoting from ?
The Public Works Act.
The hon. minister must see, if he reads it again, that it bears no such interpretation as he says. Unless it can be otherwise done better by the department-
Of which the minister himself is the judge.

Certainly; if not, who is the judge ? But more than that there is an Order in Council, to which my hon. friend probably has meant
to allude, which provides that all works costing over $5,000, and done by contract must be advertised. I cannot give a contract for any work costing over $5,000 without advertising for tenders; but if I make up my mind to carry out by day's labour any work, whatever the cost may be, I am perfectly free to do it. Whenever I give a contract for a work costing over $5,000 without tender, I must go to my colleagues; but if I want to carry out any work by day's labour, I am perfectly free to do it, and it was done over and over again by the late administration. For instance, I have often cited the case of the post office and custom-house of St. John, New Brunswick, the work on, which cost over $200,000, and was done by day's labour.
It was a case of emergency; the roof was burnt, and it had to be repaired.
Was there an Order in Council for the addition to this building ?
No, there was not, and it was not necessary. I did not give any contract for the work; I carried it out by day's labour, as I had a right to do.
The hon. gentleman has just said that he has not the right to do it without an Order in Council where the cost exceeds $5,000.

I am sorry I have not made myself understood. I cannot give a contract for over $5,000 without an Order in Council, but I can carry out by day's labour any work, whatever the cost may be, without any Order in Council. That is the law.

I am not finding very particular fault with the Minister of Public Works for doing work by day labour; but I hold that the method he is adopting is not giving that system fair play. As one who desires to see the system of day labour more generally adopted, I protest that the method at present followed in the Public Works Department is not conducive to the continuance of that system. If the day labour system is to be successful, it must be divorced entirely from partisanship ; but that unfortunately has not been the case. If it is germane to this discussion, as we have the Minister of Labour in his seat now, I particularly ask the Minister of Public Works what he has to say of the circular or letter which was sent out by the Postmaster General when acting as Minister of Public Works two years ago to his political friends throughout the country, with regard to doing work by day labour or by contract. I find that a copy of the letter, which was sent by the Postmaster General to his political friends in March, 1900, is spread on ' Hansard ' of July 13, 1900.
I may say that I never read it.
I will read two or three lines of it, and I want to know what the minister will do about it.
I will judge fairly.
I am sure he will judge fairly between the Minister of Labour and the Postmaster General.

Is it long?
In case of any work not now under contract, but authorized by vote of parliament, please state whether you advise its being carried out by contract or by day's labour.
I want to know from the minister whether the advantage that a political party may obtain by work being done by day labour or by contract is the only one to be taken into consideration, or does he think that that method of doing work should be applied ?
I want to read the whole letter. I cannot judge an important document of that kind without reading the whole of it.

The gentleman wanted to know if it was a long letter, and I wished to spare him the reading of the whole of it. But I will read the whole of it. It is to be found in ' Hansard ' of 1900, at page 10,110 :
Ottawa, March 13, 1900. My dear Sir,-During Mr. Tarte's absence I have been requested to take charge of his department for him, and it would be of great service in enabling me to take up his work if you would kindly write me at your earliest convenience with reference to the following subjects :
1. For what works in your constituency has there been a parliamentary vote ?
. 2- Have these works been begun ? If so, in what state of progress are they ?
3.	If not begun, what is your advice as to whether or not they should be begun ?
4.	Are you asking for provision being made in supplementary estimates for :
(a)	New works ;
(b)	Carrying on or completion of works already authorized or begun ?
If so, what are your views :
(a)	As to sum required ;
(b)	As to what work should be performed ?
5.	In case of any work not now under contract, but authorized by vote of parliament, please state whether you advise its being carried out by contract or by day's labour.
Yours faithfully,

YY ell, I think it is a document that is worthy of attention. My hon. friend) was new to the Department of Public Works; be did not know the work of the department as well as I did, and be wanted information, Mr. CLARKE.
and I congratulate him on bis desire to do right.
And evidently he could not get any information in the department.
I do not see anything wrong in that document. My hon. friend the Postmaster General was simply asking for advice, as my hon. friend opposite would have done under similar circumstances.

Then the idea that has been disseminated most carefully by the hon. gentleman and his friends opposite, that they believe in this system of day labour, is not very well founded. Political exigencies evidently have guided them so far, and judging by the statement of the Minister of Public Works and the letter from the Postmaster General which I have just read, there is not much hope of any reform in that direction.

I had occasion last session to call attention to the manner in which a large public work in the county I have the honour to represent is being conducted. That public work has resolved itself into an immense political job, neither more nor less. This is easy accounted for by the frank statement which the minister has made to-day. He has told us in plain terms that preference would be given on government works to the political friends of the party in power. The hon. gentleman can certainly find no fault with the manner in which that principle is carried out on the work at Wilson's Beach. When an applicant asks for employment on this particular work, he is asked whether he paws with the right foot, and it would be interesting to learn from the hon. minister if that is another of the many graphic phrases which have made his name a household word. Well, if the applicant paws with the right foot, he gets the job. Otherwise be does not. If the bon. minister is responsible for this system of selection, if be has sent out a circular to ascertain how manv people down there paw with the right foot, I would ask him to take the House into his confidence and let us know.
, There have been considerable purchases of material in connection with this work, and I doubt whether in any single instance tenders have been called-for. In the Auditor General's Report, we find one purchase of timber exceeding $8,000 and another exceeding $2,000.

Were any tenders asked? Mr. GANONG. Not so far as we know. No doubt the parties who furnished this timber pawed with the right foot. Certainly the firm of T. McAvity & Sons, which furnished supplies to the extent of $1,342, comes within this category. Has the hon. gentleman sent out his mandate that only those who paw with the right foot will be given work on this breakwater ?
The letter contains a good many clauses, but I will only read the fifth clause :

I cannot gratify my hon. friend's curiosity [DOT]with regard to pawing by either the right or left foot, but I think the House will ,'ind that his indignation is rather out of place when I inform it that we asked for tenders on this work and did not receive any, consequently I had to carry on that work by day labour. I suppqse my hon. friend, if he had called for tenders and had not received any, would not have done the work either with his right or left foot. I, however, am doing the work with both feet and both hands.
Were any tenders called for, in the case of the lumber and other supplies ?
I cannot say. Those are details that were left to the engineer.

The Minister of Public Works put his own interpretation on the Order in Council. He says it only applies to contracts over $5,000 and does not apply to work done by day labour. The hon. gentleman is the first minister to venture to put that interpretation upon it. But what does he care about Orders in Council or Acts of parliament. They are not binding on him. The words in the Order in Council are as clear as possible :
On a joint memo, dated March 20th, 1880, from the Minister of Public. Works and the Minister of Railways and Canals, recommending that hereafter all public works involving an expenditure of over $5-,000 shall be let for public tender and contract, unless, owing to urgency or other cause, it be deemed advisable to take a different action, and in all such cases authority must be obtained by Order in Council.
The hon. gentleman says he never got such authority, but he puts up the plea that while he could not enter into a contract of over $5,000 without calling for tenders, he could employ day labour to any extent.

If the hon. gentleman would read the whole Order in Council, he would find that it deals solely with public tenders and contracts. That is a view which has always been acted upon both by myself and by predecessors. It is no use trying to interpret an Order' in Council by quoting only a part of it. The hon. gentleman knows very well that there is no difficulty in any minister carrying on a work by day labour or by contract if he makes up his mind to go to his colleagues.
He gets an Order in Council.
That has never been done.
Always.

Never in the Department of Public Works. At any rate in the present instance, the
work has been given by public tender and contract.
What was the deposit ?
Ten per cent.
Who was the successful contractor ?
Mr. Harrington.
How were tenders called for ?
By advertisement in the newspapers.
In what newspapers ?
I cannot say now. If my hon. friend wants to know whether the advertisements were put in the Conservative newspapers, I can tell him they were not.
No, what I want to know is what opportunity was given the public to know that tenders were called for ?
We published all our advertisements in the Ottawa papers and in the North-west papers as well.
With regard to the Wilson's Beach breakwater, the hon. minister has said that he advertised for public tenders and could not get any. Where were these advertisements published ?
In many of the newspapers of New Brunswick and also in Ottawa, I have no doubt.
In ' La Patrie ' ?
Yes, I believe ' La Patrie ' has a very large circulation.
There has been $14,000 to $15,000 expended on that work already. Is it possible that for such a work the hon. minister could not get tenders ?
I could not.
After advertising ?
Yes, it has happened to the department several times.

I would like to say a few words on this public tender and day labour question. We on this side claim that the healthiest way of doing the public work is to advertise for tenders. The Minister of Public Works, on the other hand says that the work will be done more cheaply, by day labour. No doubt there are cases where it is absolutely necessary to do the work by day labour. It seems to me there

are many cases In which it would be more economical to do the work by public tender than by day's labour, as it is done now. In five years there has been an increase of 810,000,000 iu the cost of the public service, and possibly this system of doing work may account for some of that increase. Let me give the minister a small example in my own county. In 189G, there was a ferry across the Burlington channel. It was operated by hand, one man being in charge. Another man was in charge of the lighthouse. They received, together, about 8900. In 1896 or 1897, a swing bridge was built. It now takes four men to operate that swing bridge, although the bridge is moved by power furnished by the Radial Railway, and all a man has to do is to touch a lever. These men are paid by the day. If the contract for working this bridge were let out, as the Postmaster General lets out contracts for carrying mail over short routes, the work could be done for 8300 or .$400 a year. The bridge is not operated at night, but only from 6 a.m. to 11 p.m. The work of the bridge could be done by one man, while another could attend the lighthouse and might assist at the bridge, as the lighthouse requires not more than two hours labour a day. Yet, it now costs 81,900 to do this work, which is so much less laborious thau before, when it cost only $900. Of course, there is one gain to the hon. minister, for all the men employed there vote the hon. gentleman's ticket.

Years ago there was a ferry at Burlington channel. But before I came into office a swing bridge was placed there. I would have been glad to put it there, because there should be a swing bridge over the Burlington channel. But, as a matter of fact, I had nothing to do with putting it there. I suppose that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Smith, Wentworth) does not understand the work or he would not talk about it as he does. What is the use of talking about one man doing the work ? The bridge must be operated, and there are windy days and there are days when the strength of one man would not be sufficient. And, in any case, this has no bearing upon the question of day's labour.

There is a phase of this question of day's labour which has not yet been spoken of. Take, for instance, the work at Wilson's Beach. I speak of that because it is in my own county. Though that work had not been going on for quite a year, there has been expended for tools and other articles necessary for the workmen between 8800 and $900. By the time it is completed probably $1,500 or $2,000 will have been expended in furnishing the necessary tools and other articles for carrying on the work. This will be added to the nominal cost of the work by, perhaps, from five to ten per cent. And the hon. minister knows that when the work is done these axes and Mr. SMITH (Wentworth).
i
adzes and manilla rope and other things will not be in sight.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Ganong) is a sound business man, and he will agree that the Department of Public Works cannot carry on works without tools. This work could not be let by tender, and it is not fair to charge to this work all the cost of these tools. We are in the position of a public contractor who has a plant. Though we buy tools for a certain work those tools are used elsewhere. These workmen are electors of my hon. friend (Mr. Ganong), and surely they are honest men and are not going to steal these tools.

I can only say that the hon. gentleman will need to put up a larger building than he has ever put up yet, if he continues to do public work in this manner, because he will have more tools accumulated from works done from the Atlantic to the Pacific than could be stored in any public building so far constructed.
I understood the hon. minister to say that the new additions to the parliament buildings cost $75,000.

The chief architect, who is within hearing of my hon. friend's (Mr. Blain's) voice, tells me that the cost will amount to about $50,000, and this includes the two elevators. There will be an item in the suplementary estimates for this addition, and when it comes up, I shall be glad to give the hon. gentleman all information.
One thing I should like to learn is what proportion of this $50,000 will be wages and what proportion will be material ?
When this item is before us, I will have the information.

There is another item to which I wish to call attention in connection with this work at Wilson's Beach. I notice there is an item for Foreman Ethelbert Savage-this is during the month of June-and also for Foreman James Johnston. The minister is probably not aware, but I can tell him why it was necessary to have two foremen in doing this work by day's labour. I am well advised that they carried the timber there, dumped it into the water, hauled it up on a lot rented by the government, fitted it, as well as one foreman was able to do it to go into position. Then it was hauled down to the pier, but it was found that it did not fit so that another foreman was needed to fit it.

I can only say that the reason we employed two foremen was that there were two different works, the work of repairs and the construction of a new work. My hon. friend knows very well that two foremen would

be required, and he is only trying to make a little political capital.
Dominion Public Buildings-N. W. T. Court houses, police accommodation, &o., $1,000.
Would the minister give us some information about this item of $1,000 for court-house, lock-up and police accommodation, &c.
That is for all court-houses and lock-ups in the North-west Territories.
Then it ought to have been ' court-houses ' instead of ' court-house '.
Yes, it means court-house accommodation.
On what principle is that money expended ?

Caretakers write to the chief architect that such and such work needs to be done, and the chief architect authorizes it.
Dominion public buildings-Renewals, improvements, repairs, &e., $4,000.
What did the hon. gentleman spend last year, and in what parts of the Territories ?
We spent $1,639.41 up to the month of December.
For what was the money used ?

A great number of items : Calgary courthouse, $5 ; Calgary land and registry office, $4.40 ; Calgary post office, $53.74 ; Edmonton post office, $24.25 ; Edmonton immigrant shed, $4.50 ; Edmonton registry office, $74.80; Lethbridge immigrant buildings, $1.57 ; Lethbridge post office, $90.33 ; Land office, $2.50 ; Macleod custom-house, $40 ; Moose-jaw court-house, $20 ; Moosomin, $7.50 ; Moosomin barracks, $6 ; Prince Albert courthouse $61 ; Prince Albert land office, $75 ; Regina court-house, $416.70 ; Dominion land office, $2 ; Rossland immigrant house, $149.60 ; North-west Territories, generally, $288.
What instructions are given to the officers there ? Do they make just such repairs as they see lit ?

No, they always make requisitions, which are approved by the chief architect.
Edmonton Jail, $10,000.

I have now before Council a report asking to be authorized to purchase a site, and the site has been chosen by the Department of Justice. They see that they will be obliged in the future to have a penitentiary, and they have found a site of 150 acres. It was intended at first to have both a jail and a courthouse, but after considering the circumstances the government has concluded to build only a jail. It is badly needed. It will provide accommodation for 40 male prisoners and 10 or 15 female prisoners. I do not intend to spend more than $20,000 or $25,000 on the jail. My officers tell me that we cannot build a jail for that money, exclusive of the site. Of course I do not want to bind myself against the opinion of my chief architect, but it seems to me that with $25,000 we can build a jail.

I
understand it was originally proposed to build a court-house, and there was a report as to what that would cost. What was the amount ?
I cannot remember. I am informed that no estimate was made of the cost of both a jail and court-house.
But a vote was taken a few years ago.
Yes.
When was the land bought ?
The land was negotiated for during last August, I think, from Mr. T. McDougall and Mr. Kenneth McDonald.
How was the value of it settled ?
The late Minister of Justice conducted all the negotiations for the purchase of the site. He sent me a report telling me that he had taken an option upon this property.
What did you pay ?
$8,950. The late Minister of Justice with whom I discussed the question told me that he thought he had made a great bargain.
That the vendor had made a great bargain ?
No, he, the Minister of Justice.
I understand the hon. minister to say that in purchasing the site he purchased 150 acres. [DOT]

Yes. The Department of Justice seeing that they would be obliged to erect a penitentiary and finding a suitable site took an option upon it. It will be for the time being a kind of penitentiary because there will be prisoners incarcerated there.
I presume the Minister of Justice intends to start a model farm out there.
I suppose they will do the same thing there as at other penitentiaries. They will make the prisoners work, and it is a good thing too.
What is the population of Edmonton ?
I cannot give the exact population-1| think 5,000 or 6,000.
I will tell you the population. It is 2,626.
It is the centre of a large district.
It seems to me that the hon. minister has paid a very high price for that site if he has paid '$9,000. From whom did he purchase it ?
I have just said' that the site was bought by the late Minister of Justice from Mr. McDougall and Mr. Kenneth McDonald.
Of Edmonton ?
I suppose so. I do not know them. I only know the Minister of Justice in this case.

I suppose the building is to be put up by contract ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS By contract.
There were- no tenders asked for the site, I presume ?

No, if we must advertise for sites, I give it up. I cannot do it.

On lot 20, block 4, section 16-17, township 30, range 27. That is all I know about it.
