He is ill, I am sorry to say.
Too much election.
It makes a fellow sick at times.
Surely this building is in the same place as the court-house and jail ?
The court-house is in the town.
Have you purchased the site ?
Yes.
What has it cost ?
We have paid $75 for it. It was bought from Messrs. Nanton & Munson.
What is the size 1
The size is not indicated.
Did the Department of Public Works negotiate the purchase ?

Yes, I think so. Sites are bought in this way, since I am asked. The Department of Justice is our agent for "all these purchases. We choose a site ; the Department of -Justice is then applied to, and they negotiate, examine the title, and pass the deed.
Perhaps the non. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) will be able to tell us where this immigrant building is ?
The site of the proposed building is in the village of Red Deer, in the southern part of the village, on the east bide of the railway track.

In regard to this purchasing of sites, the explanation of the hon. minister did not seem to be altogether satisfactory. This afternoon the hon. gentleman was good enough
to state that the late Minister of Justice had undertaken to negotiate the purchase of the site for the Edmonton court-house and jail, which cost $9,000, and the hon. minister could give us no facts on which we might reach a conclusion as to whether that was an exorbitant price or otherwise. Now the hon. gentleman says that the practice is that the Department of Justice is concerned only to search the title and pass the conveyance. That is the ordinary rule. Can the hon. gentleman say how it is that this exceptional course seems to have been adopted of entrusting the Department of Justice with the work of arranging the purchase of the property ?

I have no objection to state what has taken place. Before that purchase was made I had been in consultation with the hon. member for Alberta, and we had come to the conclusion to purchase another site. The late Minister of Justice came before council with another project. He stated that it was his intention, and he thought it was good policy, to prepare for a penitentiary later on. He represented to us that he had found a site that was a very suitable one. He was an experienced gentleman, seventy years old, long in public life, and his [DOT] ol-leagues entrusted him with the matter. In point of fact the report of council by which I was authorized to purchase this site was his own. All I had to. do in connection with the purchase of the site was to ratify his action.
I think the statement of the minister is unsatisfactory. He says the transaction is the work of his late colleague, and he washes his hands of it.
There is nothing to wash.
There may be a satisfactory explanation of what at first blush seems to be an exorbitant price, $9,000, for a site of this kind.
One hundred and fifty acres of land.

I know, an enormous piece of land. There were reasons for that, no doubt, whether good or bad. We have no explanation as to why such a tract of land was required or what the intention of the department is in regard to it.

The purpose of the late Minister of Justice was to provide for the penitentiary. No doubt one will soon be required there, and in the meantime the jail will serve for that purpose. The Prince Albert jail is a kind of penitentiary-so much so that I have nothing to do with its administration. Before preparing a report under my own



signature, I had a consultation with the hon. gentleman who sits for that riding, and he told me that the transaction was in every way advisable.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Where is it located 7
A little out of the town. The hon. member for Alberta knows the place and can describe it.

At the request of the hon. Minister of Public Works, I can only say that the facts are exactly as he has stated them. The Department of Justice sent its trusted official to Edmonton and he decided that the needs for the present and the future were such as to require the purchase of a much larger piece of ground than the minister contemplated. He looked over the ground, and without any assistance from me in that part of the transaction, decided, on his own judgment, that this particular river claim-lot 20, I think-would answer the purpose exactly. He desired to secure a property closer to the town, but I objected because I did not think it desirable to have a penitentiary located too close to the town. He then decided that this property, which was the third river lot to the east of the boundary of the town, was just what was required. There are two coal mines on the property in operation at present. It has a river frontage, and is bounded by the lake in the rear. It belonged to two different parties, and is one of the oldest claims in the settlement. This official purchased the river frontage from the owner who had occupied it some twenty-five or thirty years at the rate of $75 per acre.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What is his name ?

Terence Macdonald. He purchased the rear portion, which was not in occupation, from David McDougal for $50 per acre. Or rather, he secured options on the property1 at that price. The transfer has not yet been made and the options have expired, and I am not at all sure that the department could get the property at the money now.
Does it front on the Saskatchewan river 7
Yes, east of the town.
How far from the town ?
About twenty or thirty chains.
Did that option secure the coal mine 7
Yes, subject to the present lessees holding. There are two lessees operating the coal mines, but their leases terminate in one or two years and the coal goes with the land.
What is land selling at in that vicinity 7
In some cases it goes from $7 to $10 an acre, at a distance from the town, and up to $100 per foot frontage on the main street.
I suppose the department contemplates utilizing this large acreage for farming purposes 7
For ordinary penitentiary purposes.
And also operating the coal mine 7
Well, the prisoners must be employed in some way.

It seems a very large piece of ground for a penitentiary, if we take the quantity of land devoted to other penitentiaries. It would appear as if the minister contemplated something out of the ordinary there.
Saskatoon immigrant building, $2,500.
That work is under contract for the amount of $3,300. It was let by public tender) on the 27th of October, 1901.
Why does the department not give it by day labour 7

The labour market at Saskatoon is not very large.
Yorkton-Court-house and jail, $4,000.
Will the hon. minister please explain this item 7
There is a mistake there. A mistake of the Department of Finance, I suppose.
Oh, no.
There has been a clerical error. I am blamed so often that I want to blame somebody else now.
What is the amount 7
The amount should be $9,000.
How has that been spent 7

I have bought the land. Lots 7, 8, 11 and 12 on Front Street, and lots 42 and 44 on Argyle Avenue have been bought from the Canadian Pacific Railway for $279, and lots 5, 6, 9 and 10 on Front Street, and 42 and 43 on Argyle Avenue from Mr. J. J. Smith, for $279-a total of $588 for the site.
Tenders have not been asked for, I suppose ? But this *will be done by tender ?

It will be by tender, but tenders have not been asked for.
Public Works-chargeable to income-British Columbia-Dominion public buildings-renewal, removeiuents, repairs, &c., $6,000.
What was spent of last year's vote ?
We seem to have spent $114 more than the appropriations.
Where were the expenditures made ?

Nanaimo, custom-house; New Westminster, Dominion land's office, fisheries' office; Vancouver, examining warehouse; Victoria, drill hall, Marine hospital, post office, clerk of works' office, old custom-house; Kamloops, post office; William's Head, quarantine building; and general repairs; total $0,114.03.

Concerning the Vancouver public building, which is occupied by the post office and custom-house, has the hon. minister considered any improvement in that building ?
I believe there is no question but that the building is not large enough. In fact, I understand customs officers have to occupy a different building.

I have received a petition stating the facts which my hon. friend has just stated. In this, I am bound to acknowledge that the hon. gentleman is right and that there is not enough accommodation, as in the case of other cities. But he must not lose sight of the fact that we have just completed an armoury and drill hall at Vancouver, a large and extensive building. I do not think I can extend any hope for this year, hut I am convinced that either I or whoever may be the minister next year will be in a position to adopt a more progressive policy, not only toward Vancouver, but towards other cities as welj.
Has the hon. minister caused any report to be made as to the accommodation there ?
The only report I have is that the accommodation is inadequate.
Yet, nothing is to be done.
Not this year. A new building at Vancouver would involve a very large expenditure The hon. gentleman lives there, and perhaps could suggest something. I should be glad to have his views.

I can only speak generally of the condition of things, which, I believe is really disgraceful. I have had no communication with any of the officials, but one has only to be there a short time to see that the building is quite inadequate for such a large and growing and busy community. The expression is everywhere among business men that the accommodation is very poor indeed. And, as the trade is increasing at a very rapid rate and the revenues of the country drawn from the community are growing, "the people there have been in hopes-pressure, I think, was brought to bear by the board of trade on the department-that the condition of things would be improved. I think there will be universal disappointment, if not surprise, that the minister has not found the means of improving the condition of affairs.

My hon. friend was a minister for more years than I have been. He knows that a minister cannot do everything. It Is a question of policy, a question for the Council. There are demands from all parts of the country for increased accommodation. It takes a great deal of money to carry out all these improvements. In the meantime, if my hon. friend should, later on, have any suggestions to offer, I shall be glad to receive them.

It struck me that if we could look so far into the future-and I have nothing to say against it-as to acquire an enormous tract of land that we did not immediately need, a community which gives so much into the general revenue would have a right to expect immediate action with regard to the demands which have been so long standing.
I believe that this want of better accommodation in Vancouver began to be felt in the days of the old government when our revenues were not as buoyant as they are to-dav The need to-day is all the greater aud the ground for dissatisfaction increased by the growth of the business of the city. Seeing that moneys are being voted to provide post office accommodation for communities that at present, whatever may be the hope of the future, are not paying so much into the exchequer as Vancouver is, the matter might well be brought to the attention of the minister.

I am thankful to my hon. friend for calling my attention to the case; but he should not forget that we must be prudent-we are a prudent government. At the same time, by looking at the figures, he will be convinced that we have not done so badly tor the province that he has adopted as his
home-there are pretty iarge amounts of
money in the estimates for public buildi g in British Columbia. I have already reminded him that we have just built a laige

and expensive building in Vancouver. The government will not lose sight of the requirements of Vancouver, and I think the hon. gentleman will agree that we must not spend too much, especially when we have done so well for British Columbia.

The hon. gentleman must know very well from official communications from the government of that province that they complain that this government is not doing well by British Columbia. This government is receiving enormous contributions from that province, out of all proportion to the expenditure made in it, and out of all proportion to the relative expenditure and receipts in the other provinces. That is a standing grievance in the province of British Columbia to-day, as represented by formal memorial from the local government. But it was not from that point of view that I rose to speak ; it was from a knowledge I had that one of the most enterprising portions of the province was not being well treated in the matter of public institutions. I think there is reason for great complaint. Several times the hon. gentleman has referred to the large expenditures being made, I think, in connection with the drill shed ; but I do not suppose it was ever pretended that the concession of that public building to the community of Burrard, or Vancouver, was meant to delay the accommodation they had long expressed a desire to have for a custom-house and post office.

My hon. friend may rest assured that I will not delay obtaining any necessary information a prudent minister should have before starting an important work. British Columbia has not failed to recognize lately that we have not done badly by that province. My hon. friend must admit that public opinion has demonstrated that British Columbia appreciates the efforts we have made on her behalf.

I happen to have a lively recollection of the manner in which that question was dealt with. I do not think the gentleman who was successful in the late election in Victoria would altogether endorse the position the Minister of Public Works takes. It is true that the opponents of the government complained against the niggardly treatment the province received at the hands of this government, considering the circumstances, and considering the amount of public money at then disposal. It is true also that the victorious candidate resorted to this method ot reasoning : What can you expect if you send to parliament a gentleman who is opposed to the ministers who dole out the public funds ?-that is to say, according to .the principles enunciated the other flayT
r The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. They have not read my speech.

The argument that sent that gentleman here was I think not to the credit of the government, but it was one that prevailed, namely, that this crying injustice to the province might be remedied by sending a gentleman here in accord with the government of the day, and by that means they might obtain justice where justice would be denied to a free and independent member of the House who was not giving them a slavish support. That was the argument. It was not that the government had treated Victoria handsomely in the past; on the contrary, the gentleman who won the election said that practically all that had been given to that constituency was the result of his private conferences with the ministers of the day, though he had not been clothed with authority as a representative. Of course the argument was pressed home that if he were a representative he would obtain a great deal more at the hands of this government than could a free and independent member of the House, and particularly more than a man who did not see eye to eye with them on all public questions. I do not think that any member from the province of British Columbia, judging from what I have heard there, will rise in his place and say that that province is being treated at all fairly or at all generously by the government of the day, in connection with the vast expenditures that are being made in other parts of Canada. They do not complain of these expenditures, but I think the complaint is universal that there has been and there is a shameful neglect of the very pressing interests of the province.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS My last argument then is to ask my hon. friend to be kind enough to wait until next year.
Nelson public building, $25,006.

That work is under contract for the amount of $49,900. The contract is dated January 31st, 1901. Viau & Lemoine are the contractors. Mr. Viau is from Hull, and Mr. Lemoine from Pembroke. Public tenders were asked and they were the lowest.
Did you ask for tenders in the press of the province ?
Yes.
How far has the work proceeded ?

The chief architect tells me there is another story to be put up. They have got till the month of November to complete the work. Mr. J. A. McDonald, of Nelson, is superintending the work.

Rossland public building, $12,000.

The contractor for this work is Mr. Thos. Bradbury, of Vancouver. That was also advertised in the press, and the tender accepted was for $44,050. The inspector is Mr. R. W. Gregor. It is a general public building to accommodate the post office, customs and inland revenue.
How does that compare with the New Westminster public building in price ?
A little higher, I am told.
Does the hon. gentleman include in these contracts made in British Columbia a clause in regard to the employment of oriental labour ?

No, there has never been any complaint.
Public buildings generally-construction of armouries, $37,000.
Would the hon. minister give an explanation in detail of the armouries he proposes building and state what the plan for each may be ?

The armouries that we are building now and for the completion of which this $37,000 is asked, are these : Baddeck, Victoria county, N.S., cost $4,222, by contract; Sussex, N.B., $7,095; Duudas, Out., $3,854; Kaslo, B.C., $9,700 ; Kamloops. B.C.,	$9,700 ; Nelson
B.C.,	$9,700; Revelstoke, B.C.,	$9,700.
The contracts for the armouries at Kaslo, Kamloops and Revelstoke have not yet been given out, but the tenders are in, so my officers tell me, so that the figures I have given in connection with these buildings are estimates and not the actual prices of the contracts. I may give some explanation in regard to the buildings if my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) wants it. The armoury at Baddeck is going to be a wooden, one-storey building, on a stone foundation.
May I ask the hon. minister if this is to be built by day labour?

No, the contract for the work has been given out. Mr. J. Treen, of North Sydney, is the contractor. The contract is for $2,250, but there are fittings, and so on, and that is the reason why we are asking for more money.
That will be a very poor affair. What kind of a building is it ?
It is a wooden building. These plans are prepared by the Militia Department and by my own department, the architects of both departments approving of them.
What is the size of the building ?

Fifty-eight by thirty-four, containing four armouries each 20 x 8, and each having a room for the quartermaster's stores. For the armoury in Sussex the contractors are the Messrs. Wallace Bros. The contract is practically completed there.
What military buildings are there already at Sussex ?
I cannot say. That I do not know at all. All I know is that this has been applied for and granted and is under contract.

There are no buildings at Sussex of any consequence. Thp military property at Sussex had certain farm buildings on it. It was a farm which was purchased some ten or twelve years ago and there was a house and some outbuildings upon it, but there was no building suitable for an armoury such as is being constructed now. This armoury is for the infantry and for the cavalry, a very large cavalry regiment, one of the largest in New Brunswick, and the headquarters of it is at Sussex. The rifle ranges are located there, and the annual training takes place there. It is really the important centre of military affairs in New Brunswick.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE (Hon. F. W. Borden).

speechtext: What troops are there at Baddeck ?
I do not know ; I am only the builder, let the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence answer for the military side of it.

The armoury at Baddeck is the central armoury for Cape Breton Island. The regiment there has six companies and is to be increased to an eight company battalion. It was necessary to have some place to take care of the arms and the colonel of the regiment decided, with the approval of the district officer comanding at Halifax, that that was the proper place to have it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Is it the policy of the minister to erect armouries for each battalion in every regimental district in Canada ?

That is really a question that would be better discussed on the militia estimates. However, I have no hesitation in saying at once that although that policy was decided upon when the new rifle was purchased recently, owing to the very great delay in getting suitable armouries and because the issue of the arms was kept back, it has been decided now, at once, to issue to all the rural battalions the new arms, whether they have central armouries or not.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I presume rural officers will be allowed to keep the new' arms at the company headquarters ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Has the minister had under consideration the propriety of erecting company armouries, small, inexpensive buildings, for the care and storage of these arms at the various company headquarters ?
No, but I am bound to say that in a great many cases I think it would be a desirable thing to do if it could be done at reasonable expense.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Public Works if this item includes the cost of the armoury, which, I understand, has been promised to the town of Cornwall ?
No.
There has been no provision made for an armoury in Cornwall ?
No.
Are there any troops at Sydney, or is there any armoury at Sydney ?

No.
The MINISTER OB1 PUBLIC WORKS. A contract has been let to Messrs. J. Bowman & Company for $8,870. The building is 60 x 37 feet, two stories, basement, brick on stone foundation. Dundas is the headquarters of the 77th Wentworth Regiment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Is it the purpose to spend as large a sum as this on a headquarters armoury for each rural regiment in Canada ?
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Why is the Wentworth battalion selected for such an expensive armoury as this ?

There is no doubt that the cost of this building is beyond what was estimated. Dundas is a very enterprising town and no doubt the battalion there will grow and may in time become a city battalion. It is necessary for us to anticipate the future to some extent and while we are about it, to build an armoury which will be capable of accommodating more companies than it will be necessary to accommodate at the time of erection. I was led to understand that in this section of the country there was some development, Hon. Mr. BORDEN (King's).
which is likely to become greater in military sentiment, and that it would be proper to exceed to some extent the real needs of the moment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Now that we are discussing this point, I would like to know the views of the House. My hon. friend (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) with his experience in military matters, tells us that we are erecting a too expensive building.
I have not said so.

The hon. gentleman has hinted that $8,000 is too much for an armoury at Dundas. The Minister of Militia and myself are met with constant demands for expensive buildings from military people and when we suggest that $5,000 or $8,000 is sufficient why they are ready to fly to arms. They want not only buildings, but expensive buildings, and on that score the province of Ontario does not come last.

I am not opposing the item. I am glad to see Wentworth get the best armoury it can. It will be the largest building in the little village of Dundas. But great as the boom has been in the past, if the government go on for the next one thousand years, Dundas will probably not be entitled to a city battalion. It is toying with the House to talk that way. There are six companies in the Wentworth battalion and this $8,000 armoury will probably be used by perhaps two of these companies. Of course the arms may be stored there, but the armoury will only serve one or two of the companies. Why not give each company an armoury in the different villages throughout the county at a cost of $200 or $300 each. I will undertake to put nice little armouries at a cost of $250 each to hold the arms of each company in the Dominion of Canada. You do not want a parade ground. As a rule the arms are now kept in the captain's bedroom which may be 8 x 10 feet.
Who would take care of these small buildings ?
The captain of each company is bound to take care of them under the law.
And heat them ?
They do not need to be heated.
That would not do at all.

The hon. gentleman is mistaken in saying that this armoury will only ac-

commodate one or two companies of the Wentworth battalion. The whole battalion will be accommodated at this armoury and this was arranged before the construction of this building was undertaken.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: X do not say that this armoury will not accommodate the whole battalion, but there are not more than two companies in Dundas, and I think there Is only one. Only the local company in Dundas can use the armoury except when the battalion is marching into camp.
Each company will have a room.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: How can they use the rooms when they are twenty or thirty miles from the armoury.

I wish to ask the minister if the question of erecting an armoury at Cornwall is under the consideration of the government. I understand from the local military authorities that there is a great necessity for an armoury in Cornwall, and during last session a very important delegation interviewed the minister and came away strongly under the impression that an armoury would be erected in that town. The military men of Cornwall are still under that impression. I understand that they even went so far as to select the site, and have been in communication with the minister on the subject. Is the matter under the consideration of the government ?
The question is certainly under consideration. We have received petitions and representations. As to the choice of a site I did not do anything of the kind.
I do not say that the minister has selected a site, but I understand that the local authorities have recommended certain sites.
Nothing has been done towards the choice of a site. Representations have been made, but I do not know what fate they will meet with. I do not extend any promise.

I agree with the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) that it is highly desirable to have these armoury buildings in different parts of the counties. Take, for instance, the county of Simcoe, more particularly the east riding. The headquarters of the battalion are at the town of Barrie. I am not able to say who erected the building there, but I assume that it was the Department of Militia and Defence. It is a capacious brick building, and in it are stored the arms not only of the two companies of Barrie, but that of the adjoining township. At a distance of thirty miles is the town of Orillia. It would be unfair to ask that the arms of the Orillia company should be kept at Barrie, and as a matter of 28
fact they are kept at Orillia. Then, at the village of Coldwater, fifteen or sixteen miles from Orillia, I know at one time the arms were stored over a store, a very poor and inaccessible place in case of fire. Further on, at a distance of twenty-five miles, is Pene-tang, which also has a company. Now, if there is one thing which to my mind tends to make the militia force of Ontario something of a success-and it is not as successful, I say with all due deference to military men, as it might be-it is the fact that a healthy rivalry is engendered in rifle competitions. In order to have successful marksmen it is necessary that they should have access at all times to their arms; but this is impossible if those arms are at a distance, in some cases of fifteen or twenty miles; and I quite agree with the hon. member for North Victoria that it would be desirable to have small armouries built at different parts of the counties. I am not quite so sanguine as to the cost of these buildings as he is, for I fear they would run considerably beyond the figure he has mentioned.
I think each of these companies should be made more or less of a social club. Gentlemen who are conversant with the regiments in the cities know that the great success attained by them is due to the fact that to a certain extent they are social clubs. [DOT] The armoury at the town of Barrie is fitted up as a gymnasium, and during the winter months the two companies of the town make it a place of resort; and if there were provided at the different towns headquarters not only for the storing of the arms of these companies, but with a fairly large sized room which could be. used in the winter months for drilling and also as a gymnasium, I believe the success of our military organization would be very much promoted; and I hope the minister will make provision in the supplementary estimates for the establishment in East Simcoe of such armouries as I have mentioned.
I would like to ask the minister if the architect who designed the Sussex armoury had any previous experience in designing armouries 1
The plans of these armouries are prepared by both the architect of the Militia Department and by my architect.

The gentleman who designed the Sussex armoury did not understand his business very well, because he made no distinction between the rooms set apart for the infantry company and those for the cavalry squadrons. A cavalry squadron requires a room double the size an infantry company does, because in addition to the clothing and equipment of the men there is the clothing and equipment of the horses to be provided for. I want to bring this to the attention of the minister, so that the necessary changes will be made.

I can only say that we never go on with work of that kind without the plan being approved by the Militia Department; and, as a rule, the military people in a place where the armoury is to be built, see the plans before they are carried out. If there has been a mistake there, it has not been represented to us.
I am very glad the hon. gentleman has mentioned the fact. I will make inquiries to-morrow, and see who is responsible for my part of the matter.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I would like to inquire of the hon. minister if in this vote any provision is made for building an armoury at Gananoque. We have a battery of artillery as well as an infantry company there, and I understand that a few years ago the government purchased a site there, and paid a very large price for it 1
Will the hon. gentleman tell me when it was bought ? I never bought one.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Ask the Minister of Militia. You had a drill shed there, but you tore it down and purchased a site to build a new one, but went no further; and to-day the guns belonging to the battery and the arms belonging to the infantry are stored in a lumber yard down near the railway track. I think some provision should be made for taking better care of the government property than you are doing there.
All I know is that my department did not pay for a site. The Minister of Militia and Defence thinks that perhaps a site was bought there.

I would be very pleased to see battalion armouries built as well as company armouries. When I made the estimate of $200 for a company armoury,
I had taken the precaution of consulting a good Liberal contractor. I furnished him with the sizes of what I thought would be suitable for a country armoury for forty-two men, in which to store their rifles and equipment, and he said he would undertake to put up nice little brick buildings all over the country for less than $200 each. All that is required is one room, though I would be glad to see the companies provided with such a room as the hon. member for East Simeoe (Mr. Bennett) suggests. My object is to get the whole country equipped with armouries as soon as possible; but if it were to cost $8,000 or $9,000 for each battalion, I am afraid that long as the hon. Minister of Public Works is likely to hold his job, some one else will be occupying that place before all the buildings will be completed. Reference has been made to the 77th Battalion getting this $8,000 armoury. That battalion has six companies. No. 1 company is at

Dundas; No. 2 company is at Waterdown, to the east; No. 3 company is at Binbrook; No. 4 company is at Ancaster, on the other side of Hamilton; No. 5 company is at Stony Creek, between that and Niagara Falls, and No. G company is at Glanford. In other words it was simply a large public building for the town of Dundas. I am not objecting to the expenditure if the country can afford it. I am not opposed to any expenditure on behalf of the militia, but what I do say is that the rural companies should also have their armouries.
I really do not believe, speaking as a layman, that a $200 building would be suitable.
Make it $500.
I could not believe that the country would entertain the idea of erecting $200 buildings and I would not encourage it at all.

I venture to say that more than half the arms in the maritime provinces and Ontario are stored today in buildings, the entire cost of which is not $500. I refer to the whole buildiug in which the caretaker and his family live.
That does not prove anything.

It proves that the arms are kept in the back rooms of such buildings and kept in very good condition. We require the armouries, let the cost be what it may, and do not want the battalions to have to wait ten or twenty years for this accommodation.

As the hon. minister has invited an expression of opinion regarding the desirability of expensive armouries or the incurring of heavy expenditure to erect expensive buildings for the purpose of storing arms, personally my feeling has always been against such expenditure. While I would be disposed to vote any reasonable amount to keep up the efficiency of our militia, I have never felt that it is wise to spend such large sums in building these large armouries and drill halls in different towns and villages. I can understand, of course, the ambition of towns and villages to have fine and expensive buildings. Every town, if it gets a public building, wants to have it as expensive and showy as possible. That may be a praiseworthy ambition, but is it the part of wisdom for us to give way to it ? My opinion always has been that while we should provide suitable accommodation, we should provide it at the least possible outlay to the country, and that while we should do all that is required in the interest of the militia, we should be careful not to be carried away by too great a desire for display.
We are just now engaged in re-building one of the walls of that drill shed. The wall to which my hon. friend called attention last year is being rebuilt.
Will that give any additional accommodation ?
That question is under discussion now. When the supplementary estimates come down we will know more.

I think it would be a great mistake to construct very expensive buildings, in very elaborate style, for the accommodation of the arms and accoutrements of the militia. If that plan were adopted, it would be a long time before we could obtain homes for our different militia battalions. I may be permitted to say that I have endeavoured to set a good example myself in my own county for my own battalion, by having an armoury erected there at an expense of less than $1,000, which is ample to accommodate a battalion of ten companies.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: That is only $100 a company, and I have suggested $200.

I do not want to occupy the time of the committee more than is absolutely necessary, but I feel bound to impress again on the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Militia the absolute necessity of giving additional accommodation to the military forces of Toronto in the drill shed. This is not the first time that matter has been drawn to the attention of the hon. minister. I shall not dilate on the subject, but will content myself with reading half a dozen lines from the report of the proceedings of this House on April 16th last. In that report, I quoted a letter from the commanding officer of military district No. 2, Colonel Otter, to the corporation of the city of Toronto. On the 22nd March last, Colonel Otter wrote from Stanley barracks to the chairman of the property committee.
Sir,-I have the honour to make application, on behalf of a portion of the local militia force, for the temporary use of the 'Arcade,' St. Andrew's market, for the purpose of storing guns, wagons and harness.
With the present strength of the city corps, it is impossible to find enough accommodation in the armouries, and pending the providing of such, I am compelled to appeal to the municipal authorities as no place adapted for the purpose in view can be obtained.
I cannot make a stronger appeal to the hon. minister than to read this request from the district officer commanding to the municipal authorities in Toronto for temporary 281
accommodation of guns, stores and ammunition in one of the municipal buildings. Of course the municipal corporation are always very pleased to give accommodation, if they can, to the militia forces and meet the wishes of the officer commanding in that respect, but when I remind the hon. minister that the city of Toronto gave $140,000 for the site, upon which the present drill shed stands, I think it is not unreasonable to ask that the accommodation which has been so loudly demanded by the militia force be provided as soon as possible. I have not sufficient military training to know of the relative value of small armouries erected throughout the country or of a few large ones in cities ; but I do know that in Toronto we have provided a very fine site, as the Minister of Militia knows, and there is a very substantial building on that site, and surely it would be the policy of wisdom, when you have a splendid military organization which is no discredit to the military forces of the Dominion, to provide for it reasonable accommodation. I do not desire to take up the time of the committee pressing this matter. I have done so again and again, but I appeal once more to the Minister of Militia and the Minister of Public Works that, if it be not intended to devote any part of this item, for the purpose of enlarging the drill shed and providing additional accommodation, that a reasonable sum should be provided for that purpose in the supplementaries. I make this appeal as earnestly as I can on behalf of the militia forces in Toronto.

I have already given the names of the places where this money is to be spent. The hou. gentleman has stated that the military forces in Toronto would be very glad to have more accommodation. That is the case, not only in Toronto, but elsewhere. In Montreal the militia require a good deal more accommodation. But all that is a question of money, and my hon. friends often complain that our budget is large, that the public works is a spending department, and spends too much. The facts which my hon. friend has stated to the House are not new. Under the late administration, the position of affairs was just about the same.
No.

The military strength in Toronto is not much greater to-day than it was then, and the demand that is made by my hon. friend was made then. But governments must not spend too much money, even though some of us may be in sympathy with a more expansive policy, the financial position must be considered. The brakes must be applied, and they are often applied by the Finance Minister to-day as they were in the past. The Finance Minister is right, of course, and I cannot complain.
Before all the money of the country is voted to hon. gentlemen opposite, I would like to put in a word on behalf of the best regiment in Canada, the 78th Highlanders.

The 48th.
Mr. FRASER, No, the 78th. The Minister of Militia knows all about that regiment. They are recruited from the counties of Cumberland, Colchester and Pictou. They have not a public building and never had.

They have trenches.
Mi-. FRASER. But I am willing to come next to the hon. and gallant Colonel (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) who has just spoken. I would commend to the Minister of Militia what the hon. gentleman says, that arms have to be stored in bedrooms. How can one sleep in a room where arms are stored ? But seriously, I hope the hon. minister would take into consideration this splendid regiment and that before all the rnoney for building is voted away, he will do something for this corps, who would be the first in the fray and the last out of it.

I shall not attempt to reply to the jocular remarks of my hon. friend from Guysborough, but I want to say that the 78th is a good regiment, and, in that respect it is like 99 per cent of the rural regiments of Canada. I will appeal to those who saw the review in Toronto, where the 'hay-seed' regiments, without an hour's drill from; the month of June until they paraded in front of their Royal Highnesses, held their own with the regiments of the city who have fine drill halls in which they can drill every evening. When I point out that these rural regiments who keep their arms in bedrooms and over driving sheds, and do not cost the country a dollar for armouries can hold their own on an occasion such as that, they are entitled to some consideration from the people. I have always supported the claim for armouries for the large cities, believing that the city battalions should have a place not only for the storage of arms but for drilling the men. But I do again suggest to the minister whether it is advisable to give these large sums of money for the headquarters of rural battalions, when, as the minister properly points out-I am afraid the hon. Minister of Public Works does not hear what I say. I wish to catch the ear of the hon. gentleman, for I have great faith in him, and always had. I hope he will convert the whole ministry.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Make them protectionists.
Certainly. He is educating them right along. The Minister of Finance himself will come around in time. I would like to impress upon the Minister of Public Works the policy which
the Minister of Militia has outlined, of having inexpensive headquarters and armouries which can be provided at half the cost of these large buildings he proposes.

In some of our public buildings in Quebec, we have adopted the plan of having a room for the storage of arms. For instance, in Victoriaville, we have an arrangement of that kind, and it is received with great favour.

I do not wish to take up time, but merely to say that the hon. minister was good enough to grant the regiment which I have the honour to command a room in the public building in Lindsay. I do not think it is larger than ten by twelve, and it contains the arms of the entire regiment. That is the only room which we have in the whole county.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Carried.
No, I find that the minister has given us items making a total of $53,800, and he is asking for only $37,000.
We have $27,000 in the estimates of last year.
What regiment is represented by this British Columbia armoury ?
I cannot say; I am only the builder.
Who made the request for the armoury ?
So many requests are sent in-I cannot tell all.

I may say to the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) that these four armouries are in my district. I made the request for them, and made it pretty strongly too. You must npt forget that the district I represent is nearly equal in area to the province of Ontario. So, if I have four armouries in my district, it does not necessarily follow that they are very close together. We in British Columbia are in a different position from the people of Ontario. A great part of our country is mountainous and we require not only armouries, but places where we can drill summer and winter. I do not think that any hon. gentlemen who have been in British Columbia will say that money spent in armouries in that province is not well invested. We are pretty well in the wilds, but we have a few citizens in that province who like to have reasonable accommodation as well as the people in the east. And the hon. gentleman, (Mr. Hughes) who is a colonel in the militia well knows that we sent from British Columbia to the South African war quite

a number of men-probably a larger number in proportion to our population than any other part of Canada.
Good men, too.

And good men too. And we want to keep up our credit. When we have men enterprising enough to band together, we want to encourage them to do so. 1 have been associated with the militia myself for a number of years, and I can speak feelingly in the matter. I know that is necessary, and I agree with the suggestion thrown out by the hon. member for Simcoe that they not only want a place in which to store arms, but a place to drill in, and also a place in which to meet for social intercourse. A place of this latter kind is very taking in a western city, because we have not many places in those little western towns where the men can meet together to read the newspapers and magazines, and have a little social chat after their drill. Now, I am pleased indeed with the generosity of the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Militia and Defence in giving us a drill shed in that community. True, we pay very heavily into the Dominion treasury from the province of British Columbia, and we feel in the past that we have not been getting what we were entitled to. I do not know that I would go so far as to say with one member from British Columbia that we are still complaining. We are, however, still saying that in proportion to the revenue we pay into the Federal treasury the expenditure made by the Dominion in that province is very small. However, I have nothing to complain of in connection with these drill halls that are being established in my district. I thank the minister for meeting my request in this matter. I will say this, now while I am on the subject, that in the town of Nelson where I live, the appropriation will not build a drill hall there, even according to the specifications, and I call the special attention of the minister to the fact, because I mean to approach him again for more money in connection with the Nelson drill hall. We have given in the town of Nelson two lots within the fire limits, and you all know there is a law against building a certain class of building within the fire limits. We have given two lots worth $4,000 to $5,000 as a free site to the government for a drill hall. The hall cannot be built of wood, as I believe is the present intention, for the reason that the city will not permit it to be built of wood. I am merely throwing out the suggestion, so that the minister may be prepared to see me come to him again to ask for a sum in the supplementary -estimates which will be sufficient to allow us to put up such a building as the city by-laws will require within the fire limits.
Mr. HUGHES (King's, P.E.I.) While this item is under consideration, I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Militia and Defence and the Minister of Public Works to the fact that in the town from which I come, Souris, P.E.X., we have no armoury, and yet we have there a very efficient company of artillery. I wish to say to the Minister of Militia and Defence that I think he can build an armoury in connection with the drill shed there for $200 or $250, though it would have to be a wooden building. The minister knows that the Fourth Regiment to which this company belongs has an excellent record, and I hope, now that I have drawn the matter to his attention, he will take the application into consideration and if possible provide us with an armoury. It is a moderate amount, and comes very near the amount mentioned by the member for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes). Of course it would be a wooden building, and built as an annex to the present drill shed.

AVhat my hon. friend says about the artillery regiment there I know to be absolutely true. Certainly his request is a very modest one, and even if it were not as modest as it is, I should think it was one we might deal with promptly. And as there is in the militia vote a sum for repairs and additions of this kind, if my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works is not particularly anxious to do this work, I think I may undertake to say that the Militia Department will look after it in the near future.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: If my hon. friend is short of money I will do it.
Why is it that there is no sum brought down for an armoury for this Rossland company ?

I suppose the reason is that apparently in the east the government have been buying sites for armouries, while in the west all these sites are being provided free to the government. If no selection has been made in Rossland, it is the fault of the people and not the fault of the minister; but I can promise that will be attended to.
What is the reason for the distinction between the tvest and the east in supplying sites ?

I do not know whether that distinction is general or not, but in listening to the discussion to-night I understood that sites in the east had been purchased by the government. If that is not the case, then I withdraw that remark. But I know that in British Columbia we are furnishing the sites free, and I may say that we are very glad to do so if we can

only get a decent class of buildings put up on tliem. The only reason Rossland is not mentioned is simply because they have not yet furnished the government that site, although I have requested them to do so. But that will be attended to, and then I shall come to the minister for a grant.
May I ask what is the rule with regard to sites ? Are they only purchased in certain parts of Canada, and have they to be given free in other parts ?

There has never been any fixed rule. It is very far from being the rule in British Columbia that all sites are furnished free, because I have been obliged to pay large sums of money for sites for public buildings.

I trust that the minister, now that the matter has been brought to his attention, will consider this question of company and battalion drill sheds, and if it is possible, to give each company headquarters a room in which the arms may be kept, and also a recreation room where the boys can meet for social intercourse after going through their drill. I would be pleased if the minister were to furnish us with such a building, although I am satisfied the regiment will not even ask that much, but will follow the example which the Minister of Militia and Defence says he has set in his own county.

I would be only too glad, if the militiamen will change their mind in the direction indicated by my hon. friend, because I am stating gospel truth when I say that these militiamen want very expensive buildings. Every time they come on a deputation, I am frightened, because they want so much money.
Experimental farms-New buildings and renewals, improvements, repairs, &c., in connection with existing buildings, fences, &c., $10,000.

I do not want to discuss this item farther than to urge upon the hon. Minister of Agriculture to look into the advisability of establishing an experimental farm in southern Alberta and one in the vicinity of Edmonton.

That would be a question of the extension of the experimental farm system which should not be lightly undertaken. It has been discussed several times in the House and has nothing to do with this vote which is simply for repairs.
What repairs do you intend to make ? Is this just a general vote ?
Yes, this is a general vote for repairs on all the farms.

There are some important questions in connection with experimental farms which must be dealt with, but, I presume, they will more properly come up on some other items, on the agricultural vote, or the vote for cold storage. Perhaps the hon. minister will not be prepared to answer questions now on that subject.
This vote has nothing to do with the experimental farms. There is a vote for that purpose. When we take up the vote in connection with experimental farms these questions may be discussed.
This is simply for repairs at all the farms.
It must be for repairs ta buildings on the experimental farms. It is not properly stated here.
It is for general maintenance.
I must be right, or I must be wrong. If I am right this is a general vote for repairs to buildings, fences and other things on the experimental farms.
Quite true.
And has no connection with the work carried on at these farms, for instance in the dairy ?

No.
Public buildings generally, $5,000.
I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Public Works if he can state whether the Vancouver drill shed has been taken off the contractor's hands ?
Not yet.
Could the. hon. gentleman state the amount of the contract and the amount paid to the contractor ?
I have not the information, but I will bring it down on Monday.
Showing the extras, the amount for which the contract was taken and the amount that will be paid when the building is complete.

My officers will take a note of the question and I will bring the information down.
Salaries to resident clerks of works, assistants, &c., $10,500.
Where are these resident clerks of works ?

There is one in New Brunswick, one in Mont-

real, one in Quebec, one in Ottawa, Mr. Adams, tlie man wbo has supervised tbe work in connection with this building, one in Manitoba, and one in th'e North-west Territories.
Who is the one in Manitoba ?
Mr. Cyr. There is one in the North-west Territories and one in British Columbia.
We will take, for example, a building going on in Manitoba; I notice that Mr. Cyr is clerk of the work there. Is he not paid out of the estimate for that work ?

These clerks of works, for whom this sum of money is asked, are the general officers who supervise the works of the department in all of the provinces. They have special work in cities. For instance, Mr. Desjardins superintends the works in Montreal. Mr. Cyr lives in Winnipeg and supervises the works in Winnipeg and has his eyes open also to any works around Winnipeg. Sometimes we send him into the territories. These are general officers from whom we expect service all around.
They get a salary, I presume '!
Yes.
That comes out of this $10,500 ?
Quite so.

Then how is it they get their $3 a day over and above that for superintending works ? I will take in Winnipeg, for instance, the repairs going on there :
Some carpets and wall paper, also a flag Etaff,
and ensign were supplied	Works
carried out under the supervision of J. Ernest Cyr, clerk of works, Winnipeg, Manitoba.
Then he has been paid out of this appropriation.
Take the next : Examining warehouse; he is the clerk of works there. Is his pay taken out of this vote ?
Yes, he supervised the whole of the work.
I see that he is employed on the post office as well.
Yes.
I understood that in these cases the pay of the clerks of the works came out of the vote for the particular work.
No, not in these cases.
It does in regard to harbour works.

In that case, we have no general officers. If we build a harbour at Port Hope, for instance, we employ an officer, who is not in the department. In this case Mr. Cyr is a permanent employee just as Mr. Desjardins is in Montreal. That is the reason why the hon. member for East Gray (Mr. Sproule) finds their names where he does find them.
I know, but you set a man over the building of a post office and he is paid out of the vote for that post office.
He is employed for that purpose.
If he is paid out of the vote for that building how can you pay him out of this sum ? Will you be paying him a double salary ?

No, Mr. Cyr is paid only one salary, and that salary is paid out of this appropriation. He is not paid out of any other appropriation. He will supervise three or four works but he is paid his ordinary salary out of this appropriation.

It seems to me that it is possible to pay them sometimes double salaries. I have had brought to my notice only a short time ago the fact, in regard to which I asked a question and got a reply, that clerks employed in a certain department are employed in another department at the same time and draw pay there also. The answer was that the government has no knowledge of this. I am informed that it is a fact, and that it has been going on during the last few months. I give that as a justification for endeavouring to find out whether such a thing could happen or not without the knowledge of the minister.
In this case it cannot happen.
I understood the hon. minister to say that there was a clerk of works for New Brunswick. I would like to ask if this is the gentleman who superintended the armoury at Sussex ?
No, .there is a local man at Sussex. Mr. Waterbury is at St. John. He has general supervision over the works in St. John, but at times we send him elsewhere.
The superintendent at Sussex is a local man ?

Yes.
Mr. FOWLER, Does the minister know the occupation of this man ?

I am very glad this question is asked. Since

I have been in office I have taken very great care to secure the services of a practical man in each case. I may have been deceived on some occasions, but I think I have not been. Every time that a clerk of works is to be appointed I inquire whether he is a practical man or not. When the contract for the Sussex armoury was awarded, the name of a gentleman was suggested to me, and before I apopinted him I wrote to Colonel Domville, ex-M.P. for the riding, who replied that the gentleman he recommended was a practical man. On the strength of Mr. Domville's letter, which is in my office and can be brought down if necessary, that this gentleman was well fitted to be foreman of works and a practical man, I appointed him. No complaint has been made so far as to his competency.

1 may say to the minister that the gentleman in question is a practical man in one sense, as he is a practical tailor, and a good tailor too. But so far as being a carpenter or builder, he is nothing of the sort, and has had no experience whatever along that line. He lives in the town in which I lived for a great many years, and I know whereof I speak when I say that he has no building experience whatever, except that he had a house built for him, and he may have superintended the erecting of that house. It is a very modest though respectable building, but it is not a very extensive one. That is his sole experience in the building line.

I am sorry that my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) did not call my attention to this state of affairs before now. I express my deep regret that a practical tailor has been recommended to me as a practical builder of an armoury. I remember distinctly having written to Mr. Domville-I have a copy of my letter and his reply in which he states that the gentleman he recommended to me was a practical man in building-
Building suits of clothes.

What more could I do than appoint him. My hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) should have warned me before. He is guilty and not I. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) knew all about the practical tailor and he should have warned me. In future I suppose I will have to write Mr. Domville twice.
What will you do with the tailor now?

I will not make him a present of a suit; I think I shall certainly change him. Before making such appointments I have always taken the greatest care to insure that a practical man gets the position, and my officers have received most positive instructions on that point. I am sorry that I have Hon. Mr. TARTB.
been deceived by a man.from the maritime provinces from whom good things are always expected. My hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) should have warned me, and although he is not so much to blame as Mr. Domville, still lie is somewhat to blame.
The minister must be deceived in all parts of the country, because last year he employed a painter from Toronto to do dredging.

But dredging is not made by the hand. I would hire a dredge from a medical man or a tailor provided the dredge does good work. That is different from a foreman of works. The profession of a man who owns a horse does not alter the colour of the horse.
That is a horse of another colour.

The Minister of Public Works was to some extent not to blame in this matter. As a matter of fact, I know that the minister did write, Inquiring as to the occupation cf the person who had been Recommended to him as clerk of works. However, I am not to blame in the matter-, because I was so satisfied of the honesty and integrity of the contractors, that I knew they would not go wrong whether there was a clerk of works over them or not, and it was for that reason I did not interfere, because I knew that the public interests would be well protected by the contractors, even though the clerk of works knew absolutely nothing about the business for which he was selected. I beleive the minister did his duty in the premises, but he was deceived by the gentleman who made the recommendation. In order to relieve the maritime provinces from any blame in the matter, I may say that that gentleman is not a native of the maritime provinces.

I shall inquire further into the matter, and if the man is not competent I will dispense with his services, not because of any ill-will I have towards him, but a minister cannot stand being deceived in that way.
What will you do with Mr. Domville ?
I cannot dismiss him now.

The building is finished, so that the work of the clerk of works is completed. What pay did he receive ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC W'ORKS. Three dollars a day, which is the ordinary pay to a foreman of work.
Some resolutions reported.
On motion of the Minister of Finance, the House adjourned at 10.15 p.m.


Monday, March 10, 1902.
